body: Friday, February 25 2022 — Macro · Sectors · Flows · Crypto
Information available before 2022-02-25 00:00 UTC. Prices use completed prior sessions. Prepared retrospectively; later outcomes are excluded.

Macro Stance: The first day of war delivered a textbook panic-and-reversal on Wall Street, and the close matters more than the open. Al Jazeera reported the Dow plunging more than 800 points as Russia attacked Ukraine  [1] , yet the S&P 500 finished at 4,288.70 index points, +1.50%, the Nasdaq 100 at 13,974.67 index points, +3.44%, and the Dow at 33,223.83 index points, +0.28% (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2022-02-24). The reversal is consistent with investors treating the Western response so far as a manageable growth shock rather than a recession trigger, and the bid for Treasuries may be easing the case for a more aggressive Fed. We stay Mixed: the S&P 500 is still -4.16% over five sessions, and the VIX still closed at 30.32 index points after slipping only 0.70 points.

Rates & Curve: Treasuries took the haven bid at the long end while the front end kept its Fed pricing. The 2Y closed at 1.54% and the 10Y at 1.96%, leaving 10Y-2Y at +42 bps and 10Y-3M at +164 bps (US Treasury, prior close 2022-02-24). Over 20 observations the 2Y is up 41 bps from 1.13% and the 10Y up 11 bps, a bear flattening that has cut the spread by 30 bps; over the last five observations the 2Y rose 2 bps while the 10Y fell 7 bps. The curve remains positively sloped. Reuters reported Treasury yields sliding as Russia invaded  [2] , and a Reuters commentary argued the bond market is sending flawed signals on the US economy  [3] , a caution against reading the long-end rally as a clean verdict on growth.

New / Most Important: The domestic data still support March lift-off. The Real Economy Blog charted initial jobless claims continuing to decline  [4] , even as the Conference Board said consumer confidence declined for a second consecutive month in February  [5] . The war reaches households through prices: CBS News described how the Ukraine crisis is already hitting Americans' wallets  [6] , and ABC7 Chicago reported President Biden promising to soften the blow from rising gasoline prices as much as he can  [7] . Policy is the second channel. Al Jazeera reported Biden unveiling new Russia sanctions over the invasion  [8] , and Reuters quoted the White House saying all options are on the table  [9] . Crude's verdict was restrained: Brent settled at 99.08 USD/bbl, +2.31% (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2022-02-24), after OilPrice.com reported prices soaring past $100  [10] .

Playbook ✓: Action: hold a barbell of quality mega-cap technology and US energy producers, funded from consumer discretionary and banks. Trigger: keep it while the S&P 500 holds its 4,288.70 close and the 10Y stays at or below its 1.96% close. KALB's report of a Fed governor opening the door to a half-point March hike  [11]  is the hawkish tail; if that view gains ground, cut growth exposure and shorten duration. What changes the call: Brent settling back above the $100 mark Reuters used to chart oil's journey from worthless in the pandemic  [12] , which would turn the consumer energy tax from a risk into a forecast.

Macro Stance: Europe carries the war's economic incidence, and its markets closed before the US reversal. The STOXX 600 fell 3.28% to 438.96 index points, the DAX 3.96% to 14,052.10 index points and the CAC 40 3.83% to 6,521.05 index points (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2022-02-24); CNBC reported European stocks closing 3% lower as the DAX slid 4%  [13] . Bloomberg called Russia's 33% equity crash the fifth-worst in market history  [14] . We are Bearish because the region imports the energy shock directly.

Activity & Inflation: The pre-war signal was improving: Times of Malta reported eurozone growth jumping as virus restrictions eased  [15] . Energy now overrides it. Dutch TTF gas settled at 134.32 EUR/MWh, +51.10% on the day and +92.44% over five sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2022-02-24), while Al Jazeera reported Europe's gas prices soaring 62% as the crisis put fuel supply at risk  [16] . Reuters asked how dependent Germany is on Russian gas  [17] . That mix lifts headline inflation while squeezing real incomes, which complicates the path Reuters reported toward an ECB deposit rate of -0.25% by year-end  [18] .

New / Most Important: Banks with Russian franchises took the hardest hit: Societe Generale fell 12.15% and Raiffeisen Bank International 23.14% (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2022-02-24), even as Reuters reported SocGen saying its Rosbank unit operates in a normal manner  [19]  and UniCredit saying its Russian arm is self-funded and well covered  [20] . Germany suspended Hermes export credit guarantees for Russia, Reuters reported, citing Handelsblatt  [21] , and GOV.UK published what the Foreign Secretary called the UK's most punishing sanctions  [22] .

Playbook ✓: Action: underweight euro-area cyclicals and banks with eastern exposure against energy-security beneficiaries; Reuters reported European defence stocks rising as Russia invaded  [23] , and Rheinmetall gained 3.38% to 100.05 EUR (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2022-02-24). Trigger: hold while TTF stays far above 91.84 EUR/MWh, its level 20 sessions earlier. What changes the call: gas retracing most of the +51.10% jump, which would ease the stagflation squeeze and reopen the case for European cyclicals.

Macro Stance: China meets the war shock with the opposite policy bias to the West, and that is the core of a Mixed stance. Reuters reported China's inflation slowing and leaving room for policy easing  [24] , while Bloomberg described the People's Bank seizing the moment for stimulus as the Fed hikes  [25] . Against that, the private-sector growth engines remain under regulatory pressure: Bloomberg reported Alibaba planning for a new normal of low growth as the crackdown bites  [26] . Beijing's diplomacy adds a third layer, with PBS reporting that China avoided criticism of the Russian attack and called for talks  [27] . Easing supports onshore assets; the crackdown and sanctions-adjacent risk cap offshore valuations.

PMIs & Activity: The latest activity evidence is soft. Reuters reported January factory activity contracting as COVID lockdowns bit, according to the Caixin PMI  [28] , while China Daily Global Edition reported industrial profits rebounding in 2021 as production improved  [29] . Profits are the backward-looking read; the PMI is the forward one, and it describes a demand-constrained economy rather than an overheating one. Autos are stable rather than strong: the Best Selling Cars Blog reported January wholesales up 0.9% in a stable market  [30] . Policy-directed investment is the bright spot, with Global Times reporting China expected to add a record 75-90GW of solar capacity in 2022  [31] , the kind of state-steered capex that offsets weak private demand.

Credit Impulse: Credit is where the easing bias should show first. MacroMicro's tracking of LPR interest-rate swaps  [32]  is the market's gauge of further loan-prime-rate cuts, and slowing inflation gives the PBOC cover to keep nudging borrowing costs lower. The risk is that credit is being offered into weak demand: the January PMI shows activity had not yet responded to earlier easing. BNP Paribas Asset Management framed US-China monetary policy divergence as a defining theme  [33] . The war widens that divergence, because a Fed that tightens while the PBOC eases narrows China's rate advantage, but cheaper domestic credit is exactly what property and local investment need. We would treat a clear acceleration in new loans as the trigger to add onshore cyclicals.

Property: Property remains a drag rather than a source of systemic contagion, but the drag is still deepening. CNBC reported Moody's downgrading Shimao as debt troubles drag on  [34] , and The Standard reported Fantasia being sued over a bond default  [35] . Forbes noted that Hong Kong tycoon Joseph Lau's fortune edged up despite an Evergrande loss  [36] , a reminder that developer stress is still showing up in concentrated holders' fortunes. Hong Kong adds a separate problem: Al Jazeera reported the territory unveiling a $22bn budget as zero-COVID hammers businesses  [37] . The policy response visible so far is incremental, and the downgrade cycle argues it is not yet enough to stabilise developer funding.

Fiscal, Policy & Trade: The policy calendar is the near-term swing factor. The South China Morning Post previewed what to expect from China's 2022 'two sessions' as Beijing plots its course  [38] , where growth targets and fiscal quotas set the tone for the year. Trade is being rewired by the war: Reuters reported Russia's trade flow shifting towards China as sanctions start  [39] , and Global Times quoted analysts saying Ukraine tensions will affect agricultural trade but with limited impact on China  [40] . The Atlantic Council described Russia and China as partners in de-dollarisation  [41] . The investor risk is secondary sanctions on Chinese firms that deepen Russian commerce; Moneycontrol examined what possible trade sanctions against Russia could mean for India and China  [42] , and the answer depends on whether Western controls extend to third-country suppliers.

Markets & Flows: Onshore and offshore markets diverged on the first day of war. The Shanghai Composite fell 1.70% to 3,429.96 index points while the Hang Seng dropped 3.21% to 22,901.56 index points (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2022-02-24). Platform stocks took the brunt in Hong Kong: Alibaba fell 6.67% to 104.90 HKD, Tencent 3.87% to 406.32 HKD and Xiaomi 5.08% to 14.96 HKD. In the later US session, which delivered the reversal, the KWEB China internet ETF rose 0.95% and the Alibaba ADR slipped only 0.72% to 108.93 USD, while ASHR fell 1.04%. The offshore discount reflects regulation as much as war: Reuters reported fresh fears over a Beijing crackdown driving a China tech rout  [43] , and The Japan Times reported China telling banks and state firms to report their exposure to Jack Ma's Ant  [44] .

New / Most Important: Alibaba's latest outlook is the day's key China datapoint. Modern Retail reported the company betting on international growth as regulatory pressure grows  [45] , a pivot that implies less room for growth at home. Over five sessions the Hong Kong shares are down 14.72% and the ADR 13.24% (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2022-02-24), so the reset met a stock that had already de-rated. Washington's pressure has not paused either: Reuters reported the US adding e-commerce sites operated by Tencent and Alibaba to its 'notorious markets' list  [46] , keeping a US-policy overhang on the platforms even as Western attention turns to Russia.

Playbook ✓: Action: favour onshore exposure through ASHR over offshore platform names, and keep KWEB as a tactical trade only. Trigger: a two-sessions growth target and fiscal quota that confirm the easing bias, alongside a Caixin PMI that stops contracting. What changes the call: evidence that Chinese banks or exporters face Western secondary sanctions for absorbing diverted Russian trade, which would hit onshore and offshore assets together. ⚠ Divergence: policy is easing and inflation is slowing, yet Hong Kong-listed Alibaba fell 6.67% and Xiaomi 5.08% while the Shanghai Composite lost 1.70%; the binding constraint on offshore valuations is the regulatory discount, not the cost of money.

Macro Stance: Japan is a net energy importer facing a terms-of-trade hit, which makes the war a mild stagflation shock rather than a growth opportunity. Reuters reported consumer inflation in Japan's capital perking up, with the Ukraine crisis set to add pressure  [47] . The Nikkei 225 fell 1.81% to 25,970.82 index points in Thursday's session after the holiday break (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2022-02-24), leaving it -5.42% over five sessions. SoftBank Group dropped 6.83% and Advantest 4.14%, while Tokyo Electron rose 1.12%. Reuters reported that a board reshuffle may open scope for a less dovish BOJ  [48] , but energy-driven inflation is not the demand-pull variety the central bank wants to see. Mixed.

Activity & Currency: Activity was losing momentum before the war. CNBC reported February factory activity growth falling to a five-month low  [49] , and The Guardian Nigeria News reported that GDP rebounded before the Omicron wave hit  [50] . The dollar index rose 0.99% to 97.14 index points (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2022-02-24). With the BOJ still applying negative rates, as Asahi Shimbun reported in the case of MUFG Bank deposits  [51] , while the US 2Y is up 41 bps over 20 observations, the widening rate gap is the channel through which imported energy costs can be amplified for Japanese households and margins. Fiscal room to cushion households is thin; Big Think noted that no country owes more than Japan relative to GDP  [52] . EWJ fell only 0.58% in the US session, in a session that traded after the Tokyo close and during the US rebound.

Playbook ✓: Action: prefer semiconductor-equipment exposure such as Tokyo Electron over energy-intensive domestic cyclicals, and do not rely on the yen as a portfolio haven while the rate gap widens. Trigger: Tokyo inflation feeding into BOJ communication, given the board changes Reuters flagged. What changes the call: a rebound in the next factory survey, or a BOJ that explicitly looks through energy inflation, which would favour exporters such as Toyota, down 1.53% to 2,091.00 JPY (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2022-02-24).

Macro Stance: Australia absorbed the first-day shock through its equity market and its miners. SMH reported the Ukraine crisis wiping more than $70b off the ASX in a 'sea of red'  [53] ; the S&P/ASX 200 closed 2.99% lower at 6,990.60 index points, with BHP down 6.92% and Fortescue 4.18% (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2022-02-24). The cushion is commodity exposure: higher energy and food prices raise national income even as they squeeze households. Mixed.

Demand & Financing: Household demand faces a real-income squeeze. ABC reported wages recording their worst result in seven years  [54] , and separately that a huge shortage of talent is pushing wages higher, but not as fast as the cost of living  [55] . That is why the RBA can wait: WSJ reported the RBA's Harper backing a review and the central bank declining to follow the Fed on rate increases  [56] . Grocers confirm the cost pressure, with Reuters reporting Coles flagging inflation as cost controls limited a first-half profit dip  [57]  and AFR reporting Woolworths cutting its dividend as lockdown costs crimped results  [58] . Lenders are moving anyway; ANZ said it is lifting rates on some lending and savings accounts  [59] , and Banking Day reported the RBA planning floating-rate repos with shorter tenors  [60] . Commonwealth Bank fell 2.05% to 94.71 AUD (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2022-02-24).

Playbook ✓: Action: favour energy and food-linked exporters over banks and discretionary retailers. Trigger: the ASX 200 holding 6,838.30 index points, its level 20 sessions earlier. What changes the call: an RBA pivot toward early hikes, which the WSJ report argues against, or a slide in iron ore if China follows through on the iron ore single market The Australian reported it threatening  [61] .

Macro Stance: Poland is the EU's frontline economy in this war, and the market priced it as such. Bankier.pl described a crash on the Warsaw bourse and 'war panic' on the exchange  [62] , while Miesięcznik Finansowy BANK reported every WIG20 company falling after the Russian attack  [63] . The macro problem is that the shock lands on an economy already running hot: Forsal.pl reported GUS putting January inflation at 9.2%  [64] , and 300Gospodarka reported Eurostat ranking Poland's 8.7% reading the fourth highest in the EU  [65] . A weaker zloty imports more inflation just as growth confidence weakens, so the central bank faces a harder trade-off than its western peers. Bearish.

Markets: The sell-off was concentrated in banks and in companies with direct Ukrainian exposure. The Beta ETF WIG20TR tracker fell 10.38% to 31.50 PLN and the US-listed EPOL dropped 7.80% to 17.50 USD (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2022-02-24). Banks led the decline: PKO Bank Polski fell 16.82%, Bank Pekao 14.52% and mBank 14.56%. Clothing retailer LPP collapsed 25.19% to 9,650.00 PLN, Allegro fell 13.77% and coking-coal miner JSW 13.65%. Currency stress compounded the move: Rzeczpospolita reported the zloty under pressure and at its cheapest in months  [66] , and Money.pl reported the currency losing ground after the Russian assault  [67] . Rzeczpospolita summed up the consequences of the invasion as higher inflation and a weaker zloty  [68] . The starting point was already fragile; Bankier.pl had reported the WIG20 at its lowest since May 2021 days before the invasion  [69] .

Fiscal & Politics: Fiscal policy was stretched before the war, and security will stretch it further. Bankier.pl reported the government adopting the draft Homeland Defence Act and asked whether NBP profits will finance the armed forces  [70] ; Money.pl warned that public debt will rise through the NBP and grow more costly over time  [71] . Rate hikes raise that cost, as an expert explained to Business Insider Polska  [72] . Money.pl reported Fitch's rating decision citing high inflation and problems with the European Commission  [73] . Tax politics remain noisy: Biznes Wprost reported dismissals over the Polski Ład reform sweeping through the finance ministry  [74] , and Wyborcza.pl's coverage put the war, Polski Ład and the Sejm's sitting side by side  [75] . A rule-of-law deal, which EUobserver reported Poland edging toward  [76] , would unlock EU funds and has become a larger swing factor for the fiscal path.

Corporate & Sectors: Corporate exposure to Ukraine is direct and visible. Wiadomości Handlowe reported LPP closing its Ukrainian stores and moving its office from Kyiv to Lviv  [77] , Retailnet.pl reported CCC closing its stores in Ukraine  [78] , and Bankier.pl reported Grupa Kęty halting production in Borodianka  [79] . StockWatch.pl summarised listed companies limiting their Ukrainian operations amid market panic  [80] . In banking, PKO BP's chief told Bankier.pl the group had prepared for all scenarios at its Ukrainian unit Kredobank  [81] , but Business Insider Polska reported Poles withdrawing more cash from banks, as at the start of the pandemic  [82] . Energy is the policy-sensitive sector: wnp.pl reported Russian crude accounting for less than half of Orlen's refinery throughput  [83] , and Forsal.pl reported Orlen's chief pledging to terminate contracts with those manipulating fuel prices  [84] . Orlen fell 7.68% to 62.96 PLN and PGE 8.90% to 6.57 PLN (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2022-02-24). Allegro adds a governance change, with Bankier.pl reporting that chief executive Francois Nuyts will step down  [85] .

Geopolitics & Security: The security premium is now explicit. Wiadomości Onet reported the Polish army raising its combat readiness  [86]  and a Russian strike on military facilities 75 km from the Polish border  [87] . A Rzeczpospolita poll found 71.1% of Poles believe Russia could attack Poland  [88] . Allied reinforcement is the offset: Notes From Poland reported the UK sending an advanced air-defence system to boost NATO's eastern flank  [89] , and Military Times reported American troops being welcomed in Poland amid tightening security  [90] . Foreign Policy argued the crisis is turning Poland into a strategic player  [91] , and NATO's North Atlantic Council issued a statement on Russia's attack on Ukraine  [92] . Energy security matters as much as troops: Reuters had reported the Yamal-Europe pipeline flowing east as the crisis escalated  [93] . InfoMigrants reported European countries preparing for refugees from Ukraine  [94] , a humanitarian responsibility that could also carry fiscal and labour-market consequences for neighbouring states, Poland among them.

New / Most Important: The policy question is how the NBP answers a currency shock layered on top of January's inflation spike. Miesięcznik Finansowy BANK asked how the war will affect the Polish economy and decisions on rate hikes  [95] . Rzeczpospolita reported that the MPC's February move lifted rates to their highest in almost nine years  [96] , and The Banker reported Governor Glapiński taking aim at inflation  [97] . The labour market gives less cover than before: Obserwator Gospodarczy reported unemployment rising for the first time in almost a year  [98] , even though pb.pl had reported the average wage rising 9.6% in 2021  [99] , a wage base that makes second-round inflation effects more likely. Parkiet's assessment of the attack's consequences for markets  [100]  bears on a choice between tightening into the shock to defend the zloty and pausing to protect growth and the banks.

Playbook ✓: Action: stay underweight Polish equities, with banks the funding leg against energy-security and defence exposure elsewhere in Europe; XTB.com's list of four defence-sector stocks  [101]  points to defence as a theme for local investors. Trigger: further zloty weakness and fuel-price acceleration, which Agro Profil reported will speed up after the invasion  [102] . What changes the call: an NBP response that stabilises the currency, a rule-of-law settlement that releases EU funds, and evidence that cash withdrawals are not turning into deposit flight; PKO Bank Polski at 35.95 PLN and the WIG20TR tracker at 31.50 PLN are the capitulation markers. ⚠ Divergence: higher rates should help Polish bank margins, yet PKO, Pekao and mBank fell between 14.52% and 16.82%; the market is pricing Ukraine exposure, deposit behaviour and Swiss-franc mortgage risk, where INFOR.PL reported falling optimism about settlements with banks  [103] , above the rate tailwind.

Narrative: Technology led the reversal: XLK rose 3.42% to 152.28 USD, with Microsoft +5.11%, Nvidia +6.08% and Apple +1.67% (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2022-02-24). Falling long yields likely did much of the work; Investopedia described investors fleeing stocks for gold and bonds  [104] , but the bond rally also lowered the discount rate on long-duration earnings. Over 20 sessions XLK is flat at -0.10%.

Reported: Nvidia's fourth-quarter fiscal 2022 release  [105]  remains the most recent mega-cap print, and Counterpoint Research reported global smartphone revenue hitting a record of about $450 billion in 2021 with Apple capturing its highest-ever share in the fourth quarter  [106] .

EPS Upside Watch: Cybersecurity is plausibly the cleanest earnings link to the war: CrowdStrike rose 13.01%, Palo Alto Networks 13.05% and Zscaler 10.02%. CrowdStrike's research on access brokers, their targets and their worth  [107]  describes the threat economy those budgets fight.

⚡ Breaking Convention: High-multiple software normally suffers in a crisis. Here the war pulled long yields lower and put cyber defence in focus at once, so Fortune's question of how low tech stocks can fall  [108]  has a different answer when the discount rate is falling.

Narrative: Communication services joined the rally, with XLC up 2.80% to 67.44 USD, but Meta Platforms (FB) remains the swing factor: +4.61% to 207.60 USD yet -29.54% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2022-02-24). Al Jazeera reported that Meta's plunge is unmatched among big tech stocks in recent years  [109] .

Reported: Reuters reported Facebook launching Reels globally, betting on its 'fastest growing' format  [110] , and Moneycontrol reported a pilot sharing ad revenues with Reels creators  [111] . Reuters also reported Zuckerberg unveiling AI projects aimed at building the metaverse  [112] .

EPS Upside Watch: Alphabet rose 4.00%, Netflix 6.14%, Snap 5.00% and Pinterest 8.34%. Sensor Tower reported global consumer spending in the top 100 subscription apps climbing 41% to $18.3 billion in 2021  [113] , support for subscription models over pure advertising if fuel prices squeeze marketing budgets.

⚡ Breaking Convention: Telecoms, the textbook defensive, lagged: AT&T fell 1.19% and Verizon 1.54%. In this war rally the market paid for growth platforms over bond-like carriers, the reverse of the standard crisis playbook.

Narrative: Financials failed to join the rebound: XLF fell 1.20% to 37.88 USD while the S&P 500 gained 1.50%. JPMorgan dropped 2.78%, Citigroup 4.03% and Bank of America 2.64% (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2022-02-24). A curve at +42 bps that has bear-flattened over 20 observations caps the margin upside banks were promised from lift-off.

Reported: Reuters reported RBC profit rising on wealth and loan growth while flagging a mortgage slowdown  [114] , and the Financial Times reported Morgan Stanley disclosing twin probes into big stock transactions  [115] ; Morgan Stanley fell 1.86%.

EPS Upside Watch: Net interest income remains the upside lever if the Fed moves in March. A Federal Reserve note on the drivers of bank supply of business loans  [116]  is a reminder that business lending is one channel through which a March hike would reach bank earnings.

⚡ Breaking Convention: Rate hikes are supposed to help banks. Here sanctions compliance and counterparty risk dominate; the Association of Certified Financial Crime Specialists warned that sanctions, AML and cyber risks soar  [117] . Russian exposure is an operating cost before it becomes a credit loss.

Narrative: Energy equities lagged the commodity: XLE fell 0.78% to 67.11 USD while Brent rose 2.31% to 99.08 USD/bbl and WTI 0.77% to 92.81 USD/bbl (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2022-02-24). Reuters reported oil topping $105 as Russia invaded  [118] , before crude gave back much of that spike into the settlement.

Reported: BBC reported oil hitting a seven-year high even as shares rebounded  [119] . Reuters reported Chevron monitoring the Russia situation and saying it can adjust crude supply  [120] , while Saipem tempered its green ambitions after a loss prompted a rethink  [121] .

EPS Upside Watch: With Brent +10.14% over 20 sessions against XLE's +2.93%, equities price only a fraction of the strip. Exxon Mobil fell 1.26%, Chevron 0.52% and Schlumberger 3.57%, which could leave room for estimates to catch up with crude if prices hold.

⚡ Breaking Convention: Integrated majors fell on the day GMA Network reported oil rising above $105 after the attack  [122] ; money moved toward technology on the day while energy equities slipped. That gap between commodity and equity is an opportunity, not a warning.

Narrative: Industrials rose 1.28% to 96.82 USD, led by defence: Lockheed Martin +1.75%, Northrop Grumman +2.44%, Raytheon Technologies (RTX) +2.18% and the ITA ETF +2.75% (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2022-02-24). Reuters reported BAE Systems saying the Russian invasion will sharpen the focus on defence  [123] , and Fortune reported Reddit's WallStreetBets celebrating war-friendly stocks  [124] .

Reported: Safran reported its full-year 2021 results  [125]  and, per Reuters, boosted titanium stocks to shore up its supply chain  [126] . Bloomberg reported jet-engine makers looking for titanium supplies outside Russia  [127] .

EPS Upside Watch: Quanta Services rose 10.60%, while Caterpillar fell 1.06% and is -13.81% over 20 sessions, so the rally was selective. Deere, which Reuters said aims for bigger profit as price hikes powered an earnings beat  [128] , rose 1.55%.

⚡ Breaking Convention: Aerospace is not a clean war winner. Airbus fell 4.41% and Boeing has lost 9.36% over five sessions; CNN had reported airlines cancelling Ukraine flights as the threat of war grew  [129] . Titanium dependence and route disruption cut against defence budgets inside the same sector.

Narrative: Consumer discretionary bounced 2.29% to 172.77 USD on Amazon +4.51% and Tesla +4.81%, but is -7.16% over five sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2022-02-24). Fuel is the war's main channel to households, and The Conversation warned of higher food and gas prices and an increased risk of recession  [130] .

Reported: The Business of Fashion reported TJX results missing estimates due to Omicron store closures  [131] ; Bloomberg reported eBay warning it is still losing customers  [132] ; Retail Dive reported Wayfair's revenue falling 11.4% in the fourth quarter as losses widened  [133] .

EPS Upside Watch: Home improvement is holding up: Reuters reported Lowe's optimistic on demand despite rising interest rates  [134] . Auto Remarketing reported KAR selling its ADESA US physical auction business to Carvana for $2.2B  [135] ; Carvana rose 10.91%. The Verge reported Etsy hitting sellers with a 30 percent transaction-fee increase  [136] , a platform testing its pricing power.

⚡ Breaking Convention: The rebound was led by mega-cap platforms, not by the household. With confidence falling and fuel prices rising, discretionary spending faces a tax that the index rally ignored.

Narrative: Staples were a funding leg: XLP fell 1.72% to 73.54 USD while the S&P 500 rose, with Procter & Gamble -2.69%, Coca-Cola -1.75% and PepsiCo -1.74% (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2022-02-24). Investors sold defensives to buy beta, a rotation that works only if the energy shock stays contained; Walmart slipped 0.39%.

Reported: Reuters reported Coca-Cola HBC readying Russia contingencies as profits rose  [137]  and then shutting its Ukraine plant  [138] . Reuters also reported Nestle temporarily closing factories and warehouses in Ukraine  [139] ; Nestle fell 3.15% to 115.16 CHF.

EPS Upside Watch: Pricing power is the swing factor. CBC reported more shoppers feeling inflation pressure and turning to dollar stores for deals  [140] , while Costco rose 2.08%, a sign that value formats can take share as budgets tighten. CSP Daily News reported private labels lifting US sales to $199 billion in 2021  [141] , a structural base for trading down.

Historical Analog: The cautionary tale arrived in the same session, on the other side of the same trade. Russian stocks crashed 33% and the ruble plunged to a record low  [251] ; Bloomberg ranks the 33% crash as the fifth-worst in market history  [14] , erasing $150 billion in value  [214] . Anyone who followed the reported flows into both Russian equities and defence owned a pair that split violently, one leg gutted and the other higher. The mechanism matters for the surviving leg. War premiums tend to be paid up front on expectations of bigger budgets, while contracts and revenue arrive over years, so prices can run far ahead of anything a quarterly report can confirm.

Smart Money View: The industry and the money are telling different stories. BAE Systems says the invasion will sharpen the focus on defence  [123] , the bull case in management's own words. Much of the haven bid went elsewhere: Investopedia describes investors fleeing stocks for the refuge of gold and bonds  [104] , Reuters reports big inflows into gold ETFs on rising geopolitical concerns  [187] , and the 10Y yield sits at 1.96%, 7 bps lower over five observations, with the 2Y at 1.54% (US Treasury, prior close 2022-02-24). Even that trade comes with a caution, CNBC suggesting buyers may want to resist the rush into gold  [252] . JPMorgan's Natasha Kaneva has been walking CNBC viewers through how sanctions feed into commodities  [253] , the channel that decides what contractors pay for inputs. The scoreboard is modest: ITA is still down 2.32% over five sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2022-02-24), bounced rather than re-rated.

When the Narrative Breaks: The war trade breaks on the same news that would relieve everyone else: a ceasefire or negotiated pause would drain the premium before any new budget is passed. It also breaks if the tech rebound keeps running, because money that came into defence as a hiding place can leave as fast as it arrived. The level to watch is ITA's $100.77 close of twenty sessions earlier: a slide back below it would say the invasion premium is gone (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2022-02-24). Sanctions are the wild card. The White House says all options are on the table  [9] , and Reuters reports Safran boosting its titanium stocks to shore up its supply chain  [126] , a reminder that measures which push up metal inputs raise costs for the same contractors the crowd is buying.

Why Retail Is Here: The leveraged dip-buy got its answer inside one session. Al Jazeera had the Dow plunging more than 800 points as Russia attacked  [1] , yet it closed 0.28% higher, and TQQQ jumped 9.79% to $49.56 as the Nasdaq 100 rose 3.44% to 13,974.67 index points, with ARKK up 7.79% and AMC up 12.40% (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2022-02-24). A session that opened in panic closed with the Nasdaq 100 up 3.44%, exactly the reversal the dip-buying crowd waits for. For dip-buyers it is vindication, the kind that tends to encourage a bigger bet next time.

Where It Breaks: One green day does not repair a bruising week. TQQQ is still down 13.49% over five sessions, and the VIX at 30.32 is only 0.70 points lower, nowhere near calm (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2022-02-24). The rebound came on a day of fresh sanctions, not a resolution, and the daily leverage that amplified the bounce will amplify the next drop.

Why Retail Is Here: Tesla is the crowd's longest-running faith trade, and the regulator story has moved from Musk's complaints to Musk's own trades. The Wall Street Journal reports the SEC is probing trading by Elon Musk and his brother in the wake of the chief executive's share sales  [247] ; the shares, swept up in the Nasdaq rebound, rose 4.81% to $800.77 on the session (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2022-02-24). Believers have a counter-headline: Reuters, citing sources, reports Tesla plans a new Shanghai plant to more than double its China capacity  [246] . For the faithful, regulators are noise and capacity is destiny.

Where It Breaks: The bounce rode a Nasdaq rebound, not a verdict. The Guardian describes the probe as an investigation into alleged insider trading  [254] , a question no capacity headline answers. The shares are still down 13.28% over five sessions and 14.58% over twenty, from $937.41 (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2022-02-24), and YourStory counts more than $140B lost from Musk's fortune in four months  [255] , so the wealth effect runs both ways. The tell is relative: if Tesla gives back its 4.81% while the Nasdaq holds, the probe, not the market, is setting the price.

Why Retail Is Here: Coinbase is how much of the crypto crowd buys, so its results double as a census. The quarter impressed, with CNBC reporting a big revenue beat  [177] , but Bloomberg's headline pairs the beat with a caution on trading volume  [196] . The shares had closed up 3.95% at $179.56 in the regular session, still down 13.66% over five (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2022-02-24). Bitcoin ended the UTC day 2.78% higher at $38,332.61 (Yahoo Finance, prior completed daily close 2022-02-24) after a slide that Yahoo Finance UK said blew its safe-haven claims to bits  [191] .

Where It Breaks: The bull case says a volatile war tape brings traders back; the company's own outlook, which CNBC says expects first-quarter trading volume to fall  [177] , says the opposite. When volumes fall, a broker's link to retail enthusiasm works in reverse, and bitcoin's 7.63% slide over 20 sessions from $41,500.88 (Yahoo Finance, prior completed daily close 2022-02-24) suggests that enthusiasm is already thinner. A bitcoin bounce that fails to revive trading would confirm a crowd that is watching rather than playing.

geo.label: March lift-off intact, war caps the pace
parts: Macro Stance

The first day of war delivered a textbook panic-and-reversal on Wall Street, and the close matters more than the open. Al Jazeera reported the Dow plunging more than 800 points as Russia attacked Ukraine [[n1126]], yet the S&P 500 finished at 4,288.70 index points, +1.50%, the Nasdaq 100 at 13,974.67 index points, +3.44%, and the Dow at 33,223.83 index points, +0.28% (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2022-02-24). The reversal is consistent with investors treating the Western response so far as a manageable growth shock rather than a recession trigger, and the bid for Treasuries may be easing the case for a more aggressive Fed. We stay Mixed: the S&P 500 is still -4.16% over five sessions, and the VIX still closed at 30.32 index points after slipping only 0.70 points.
Rates & Curve

Treasuries took the haven bid at the long end while the front end kept its Fed pricing. The 2Y closed at 1.54% and the 10Y at 1.96%, leaving 10Y-2Y at +42 bps and 10Y-3M at +164 bps (US Treasury, prior close 2022-02-24). Over 20 observations the 2Y is up 41 bps from 1.13% and the 10Y up 11 bps, a bear flattening that has cut the spread by 30 bps; over the last five observations the 2Y rose 2 bps while the 10Y fell 7 bps. The curve remains positively sloped. Reuters reported Treasury yields sliding as Russia invaded [[n0241]], and a Reuters commentary argued the bond market is sending flawed signals on the US economy [[n1965]], a caution against reading the long-end rally as a clean verdict on growth.
New / Most Important

The domestic data still support March lift-off. The Real Economy Blog charted initial jobless claims continuing to decline [[n1909]], even as the Conference Board said consumer confidence declined for a second consecutive month in February [[n1906]]. The war reaches households through prices: CBS News described how the Ukraine crisis is already hitting Americans' wallets [[n1257]], and ABC7 Chicago reported President Biden promising to soften the blow from rising gasoline prices as much as he can [[n1300]]. Policy is the second channel. Al Jazeera reported Biden unveiling new Russia sanctions over the invasion [[n1281]], and Reuters quoted the White House saying all options are on the table [[n0227]]. Crude's verdict was restrained: Brent settled at 99.08 USD/bbl, +2.31% (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2022-02-24), after OilPrice.com reported prices soaring past $100 [[n1772]].
Playbook ✓

Action: hold a barbell of quality mega-cap technology and US energy producers, funded from consumer discretionary and banks. Trigger: keep it while the S&P 500 holds its 4,288.70 close and the 10Y stays at or below its 1.96% close. KALB's report of a Fed governor opening the door to a half-point March hike [[n1941]] is the hawkish tail; if that view gains ground, cut growth exposure and shorten duration. What changes the call: Brent settling back above the $100 mark Reuters used to chart oil's journey from worthless in the pandemic [[n0743]], which would turn the consumer energy tax from a risk into a forecast.

geo.label: Gas shock collides with ECB normalisation
parts: Macro Stance

Europe carries the war's economic incidence, and its markets closed before the US reversal. The STOXX 600 fell 3.28% to 438.96 index points, the DAX 3.96% to 14,052.10 index points and the CAC 40 3.83% to 6,521.05 index points (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2022-02-24); CNBC reported European stocks closing 3% lower as the DAX slid 4% [[n0691]]. Bloomberg called Russia's 33% equity crash the fifth-worst in market history [[n0762]]. We are Bearish because the region imports the energy shock directly.
Activity & Inflation

The pre-war signal was improving: Times of Malta reported eurozone growth jumping as virus restrictions eased [[n1059]]. Energy now overrides it. Dutch TTF gas settled at 134.32 EUR/MWh, +51.10% on the day and +92.44% over five sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2022-02-24), while Al Jazeera reported Europe's gas prices soaring 62% as the crisis put fuel supply at risk [[n1127]]. Reuters asked how dependent Germany is on Russian gas [[n1130]]. That mix lifts headline inflation while squeezing real incomes, which complicates the path Reuters reported toward an ECB deposit rate of -0.25% by year-end [[n1040]].
New / Most Important

Banks with Russian franchises took the hardest hit: Societe Generale fell 12.15% and Raiffeisen Bank International 23.14% (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2022-02-24), even as Reuters reported SocGen saying its Rosbank unit operates in a normal manner [[n0774]] and UniCredit saying its Russian arm is self-funded and well covered [[n0794]]. Germany suspended Hermes export credit guarantees for Russia, Reuters reported, citing Handelsblatt [[n0704]], and GOV.UK published what the Foreign Secretary called the UK's most punishing sanctions [[n1286]].
Playbook ✓

Action: underweight euro-area cyclicals and banks with eastern exposure against energy-security beneficiaries; Reuters reported European defence stocks rising as Russia invaded [[n0690]], and Rheinmetall gained 3.38% to 100.05 EUR (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2022-02-24). Trigger: hold while TTF stays far above 91.84 EUR/MWh, its level 20 sessions earlier. What changes the call: gas retracing most of the +51.10% jump, which would ease the stagflation squeeze and reopen the case for European cyclicals.

geo.label: Easing bias versus the regulatory discount
parts: Macro Stance

China meets the war shock with the opposite policy bias to the West, and that is the core of a Mixed stance. Reuters reported China's inflation slowing and leaving room for policy easing [[n0162]], while Bloomberg described the People's Bank seizing the moment for stimulus as the Fed hikes [[n0147]]. Against that, the private-sector growth engines remain under regulatory pressure: Bloomberg reported Alibaba planning for a new normal of low growth as the crackdown bites [[n0229]]. Beijing's diplomacy adds a third layer, with PBS reporting that China avoided criticism of the Russian attack and called for talks [[n1284]]. Easing supports onshore assets; the crackdown and sanctions-adjacent risk cap offshore valuations.
PMIs & Activity

The latest activity evidence is soft. Reuters reported January factory activity contracting as COVID lockdowns bit, according to the Caixin PMI [[n0152]], while China Daily Global Edition reported industrial profits rebounding in 2021 as production improved [[n0150]]. Profits are the backward-looking read; the PMI is the forward one, and it describes a demand-constrained economy rather than an overheating one. Autos are stable rather than strong: the Best Selling Cars Blog reported January wholesales up 0.9% in a stable market [[n0195]]. Policy-directed investment is the bright spot, with Global Times reporting China expected to add a record 75-90GW of solar capacity in 2022 [[n0214]], the kind of state-steered capex that offsets weak private demand.
Credit Impulse

Credit is where the easing bias should show first. MacroMicro's tracking of LPR interest-rate swaps [[n0154]] is the market's gauge of further loan-prime-rate cuts, and slowing inflation gives the PBOC cover to keep nudging borrowing costs lower. The risk is that credit is being offered into weak demand: the January PMI shows activity had not yet responded to earlier easing. BNP Paribas Asset Management framed US-China monetary policy divergence as a defining theme [[n1141]]. The war widens that divergence, because a Fed that tightens while the PBOC eases narrows China's rate advantage, but cheaper domestic credit is exactly what property and local investment need. We would treat a clear acceleration in new loans as the trigger to add onshore cyclicals.
Property

Property remains a drag rather than a source of systemic contagion, but the drag is still deepening. CNBC reported Moody's downgrading Shimao as debt troubles drag on [[n0238]], and The Standard reported Fantasia being sued over a bond default [[n0203]]. Forbes noted that Hong Kong tycoon Joseph Lau's fortune edged up despite an Evergrande loss [[n0219]], a reminder that developer stress is still showing up in concentrated holders' fortunes. Hong Kong adds a separate problem: Al Jazeera reported the territory unveiling a $22bn budget as zero-COVID hammers businesses [[n0220]]. The policy response visible so far is incremental, and the downgrade cycle argues it is not yet enough to stabilise developer funding.
Fiscal, Policy & Trade

The policy calendar is the near-term swing factor. The South China Morning Post previewed what to expect from China's 2022 'two sessions' as Beijing plots its course [[n0245]], where growth targets and fiscal quotas set the tone for the year. Trade is being rewired by the war: Reuters reported Russia's trade flow shifting towards China as sanctions start [[n0192]], and Global Times quoted analysts saying Ukraine tensions will affect agricultural trade but with limited impact on China [[n0242]]. The Atlantic Council described Russia and China as partners in de-dollarisation [[n0168]]. The investor risk is secondary sanctions on Chinese firms that deepen Russian commerce; Moneycontrol examined what possible trade sanctions against Russia could mean for India and China [[n0226]], and the answer depends on whether Western controls extend to third-country suppliers.
Markets & Flows

Onshore and offshore markets diverged on the first day of war. The Shanghai Composite fell 1.70% to 3,429.96 index points while the Hang Seng dropped 3.21% to 22,901.56 index points (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2022-02-24). Platform stocks took the brunt in Hong Kong: Alibaba fell 6.67% to 104.90 HKD, Tencent 3.87% to 406.32 HKD and Xiaomi 5.08% to 14.96 HKD. In the later US session, which delivered the reversal, the KWEB China internet ETF rose 0.95% and the Alibaba ADR slipped only 0.72% to 108.93 USD, while ASHR fell 1.04%. The offshore discount reflects regulation as much as war: Reuters reported fresh fears over a Beijing crackdown driving a China tech rout [[n0204]], and The Japan Times reported China telling banks and state firms to report their exposure to Jack Ma's Ant [[n0194]].
New / Most Important

Alibaba's latest outlook is the day's key China datapoint. Modern Retail reported the company betting on international growth as regulatory pressure grows [[n0660]], a pivot that implies less room for growth at home. Over five sessions the Hong Kong shares are down 14.72% and the ADR 13.24% (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2022-02-24), so the reset met a stock that had already de-rated. Washington's pressure has not paused either: Reuters reported the US adding e-commerce sites operated by Tencent and Alibaba to its 'notorious markets' list [[n0170]], keeping a US-policy overhang on the platforms even as Western attention turns to Russia.
Playbook ✓

Action: favour onshore exposure through ASHR over offshore platform names, and keep KWEB as a tactical trade only. Trigger: a two-sessions growth target and fiscal quota that confirm the easing bias, alongside a Caixin PMI that stops contracting. What changes the call: evidence that Chinese banks or exporters face Western secondary sanctions for absorbing diverted Russian trade, which would hit onshore and offshore assets together. ⚠ Divergence: policy is easing and inflation is slowing, yet Hong Kong-listed Alibaba fell 6.67% and Xiaomi 5.08% while the Shanghai Composite lost 1.70%; the binding constraint on offshore valuations is the regulatory discount, not the cost of money.

geo.label: Imported inflation tests a patient BOJ
parts: Macro Stance

Japan is a net energy importer facing a terms-of-trade hit, which makes the war a mild stagflation shock rather than a growth opportunity. Reuters reported consumer inflation in Japan's capital perking up, with the Ukraine crisis set to add pressure [[n0989]]. The Nikkei 225 fell 1.81% to 25,970.82 index points in Thursday's session after the holiday break (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2022-02-24), leaving it -5.42% over five sessions. SoftBank Group dropped 6.83% and Advantest 4.14%, while Tokyo Electron rose 1.12%. Reuters reported that a board reshuffle may open scope for a less dovish BOJ [[n1331]], but energy-driven inflation is not the demand-pull variety the central bank wants to see. Mixed.
Activity & Currency

Activity was losing momentum before the war. CNBC reported February factory activity growth falling to a five-month low [[n1337]], and The Guardian Nigeria News reported that GDP rebounded before the Omicron wave hit [[n1329]]. The dollar index rose 0.99% to 97.14 index points (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2022-02-24). With the BOJ still applying negative rates, as Asahi Shimbun reported in the case of MUFG Bank deposits [[n1323]], while the US 2Y is up 41 bps over 20 observations, the widening rate gap is the channel through which imported energy costs can be amplified for Japanese households and margins. Fiscal room to cushion households is thin; Big Think noted that no country owes more than Japan relative to GDP [[n1325]]. EWJ fell only 0.58% in the US session, in a session that traded after the Tokyo close and during the US rebound.
Playbook ✓

Action: prefer semiconductor-equipment exposure such as Tokyo Electron over energy-intensive domestic cyclicals, and do not rely on the yen as a portfolio haven while the rate gap widens. Trigger: Tokyo inflation feeding into BOJ communication, given the board changes Reuters flagged. What changes the call: a rebound in the next factory survey, or a BOJ that explicitly looks through energy inflation, which would favour exporters such as Toyota, down 1.53% to 2,091.00 JPY (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2022-02-24).

geo.label: RBA patience, commodity cushion
parts: Macro Stance

Australia absorbed the first-day shock through its equity market and its miners. SMH reported the Ukraine crisis wiping more than $70b off the ASX in a 'sea of red' [[n1317]]; the S&P/ASX 200 closed 2.99% lower at 6,990.60 index points, with BHP down 6.92% and Fortescue 4.18% (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2022-02-24). The cushion is commodity exposure: higher energy and food prices raise national income even as they squeeze households. Mixed.
Demand & Financing

Household demand faces a real-income squeeze. ABC reported wages recording their worst result in seven years [[n0086]], and separately that a huge shortage of talent is pushing wages higher, but not as fast as the cost of living [[n0047]]. That is why the RBA can wait: WSJ reported the RBA's Harper backing a review and the central bank declining to follow the Fed on rate increases [[n0027]]. Grocers confirm the cost pressure, with Reuters reporting Coles flagging inflation as cost controls limited a first-half profit dip [[n0041]] and AFR reporting Woolworths cutting its dividend as lockdown costs crimped results [[n0070]]. Lenders are moving anyway; ANZ said it is lifting rates on some lending and savings accounts [[n0073]], and Banking Day reported the RBA planning floating-rate repos with shorter tenors [[n0063]]. Commonwealth Bank fell 2.05% to 94.71 AUD (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2022-02-24).
Playbook ✓

Action: favour energy and food-linked exporters over banks and discretionary retailers. Trigger: the ASX 200 holding 6,838.30 index points, its level 20 sessions earlier. What changes the call: an RBA pivot toward early hikes, which the WSJ report argues against, or a slide in iron ore if China follows through on the iron ore single market The Australian reported it threatening [[n0050]].

geo.label: Frontline risk premium, NBP squeezed
parts: Macro Stance

Poland is the EU's frontline economy in this war, and the market priced it as such. Bankier.pl described a crash on the Warsaw bourse and 'war panic' on the exchange [[n1536]], while Miesięcznik Finansowy BANK reported every WIG20 company falling after the Russian attack [[n1542]]. The macro problem is that the shock lands on an economy already running hot: Forsal.pl reported GUS putting January inflation at 9.2% [[n1404]], and 300Gospodarka reported Eurostat ranking Poland's 8.7% reading the fourth highest in the EU [[n1500]]. A weaker zloty imports more inflation just as growth confidence weakens, so the central bank faces a harder trade-off than its western peers. Bearish.
Markets

The sell-off was concentrated in banks and in companies with direct Ukrainian exposure. The Beta ETF WIG20TR tracker fell 10.38% to 31.50 PLN and the US-listed EPOL dropped 7.80% to 17.50 USD (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2022-02-24). Banks led the decline: PKO Bank Polski fell 16.82%, Bank Pekao 14.52% and mBank 14.56%. Clothing retailer LPP collapsed 25.19% to 9,650.00 PLN, Allegro fell 13.77% and coking-coal miner JSW 13.65%. Currency stress compounded the move: Rzeczpospolita reported the zloty under pressure and at its cheapest in months [[n1571]], and Money.pl reported the currency losing ground after the Russian assault [[n1572]]. Rzeczpospolita summed up the consequences of the invasion as higher inflation and a weaker zloty [[n1556]]. The starting point was already fragile; Bankier.pl had reported the WIG20 at its lowest since May 2021 days before the invasion [[n1447]].
Fiscal & Politics

Fiscal policy was stretched before the war, and security will stretch it further. Bankier.pl reported the government adopting the draft Homeland Defence Act and asked whether NBP profits will finance the armed forces [[n1481]]; Money.pl warned that public debt will rise through the NBP and grow more costly over time [[n1422]]. Rate hikes raise that cost, as an expert explained to Business Insider Polska [[n1429]]. Money.pl reported Fitch's rating decision citing high inflation and problems with the European Commission [[n1424]]. Tax politics remain noisy: Biznes Wprost reported dismissals over the Polski Ład reform sweeping through the finance ministry [[n1439]], and Wyborcza.pl's coverage put the war, Polski Ład and the Sejm's sitting side by side [[n1564]]. A rule-of-law deal, which EUobserver reported Poland edging toward [[n1362]], would unlock EU funds and has become a larger swing factor for the fiscal path.
Corporate & Sectors

Corporate exposure to Ukraine is direct and visible. Wiadomości Handlowe reported LPP closing its Ukrainian stores and moving its office from Kyiv to Lviv [[n1555]], Retailnet.pl reported CCC closing its stores in Ukraine [[n1524]], and Bankier.pl reported Grupa Kęty halting production in Borodianka [[n1532]]. StockWatch.pl summarised listed companies limiting their Ukrainian operations amid market panic [[n1547]]. In banking, PKO BP's chief told Bankier.pl the group had prepared for all scenarios at its Ukrainian unit Kredobank [[n1546]], but Business Insider Polska reported Poles withdrawing more cash from banks, as at the start of the pandemic [[n1543]]. Energy is the policy-sensitive sector: wnp.pl reported Russian crude accounting for less than half of Orlen's refinery throughput [[n1562]], and Forsal.pl reported Orlen's chief pledging to terminate contracts with those manipulating fuel prices [[n1523]]. Orlen fell 7.68% to 62.96 PLN and PGE 8.90% to 6.57 PLN (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2022-02-24). Allegro adds a governance change, with Bankier.pl reporting that chief executive Francois Nuyts will step down [[n1530]].
Geopolitics & Security

The security premium is now explicit. Wiadomości Onet reported the Polish army raising its combat readiness [[n1563]] and a Russian strike on military facilities 75 km from the Polish border [[n1553]]. A Rzeczpospolita poll found 71.1% of Poles believe Russia could attack Poland [[n1557]]. Allied reinforcement is the offset: Notes From Poland reported the UK sending an advanced air-defence system to boost NATO's eastern flank [[n1382]], and Military Times reported American troops being welcomed in Poland amid tightening security [[n1379]]. Foreign Policy argued the crisis is turning Poland into a strategic player [[n1372]], and NATO's North Atlantic Council issued a statement on Russia's attack on Ukraine [[n1304]]. Energy security matters as much as troops: Reuters had reported the Yamal-Europe pipeline flowing east as the crisis escalated [[n1081]]. InfoMigrants reported European countries preparing for refugees from Ukraine [[n1371]], a humanitarian responsibility that could also carry fiscal and labour-market consequences for neighbouring states, Poland among them.
New / Most Important

The policy question is how the NBP answers a currency shock layered on top of January's inflation spike. Miesięcznik Finansowy BANK asked how the war will affect the Polish economy and decisions on rate hikes [[n1533]]. Rzeczpospolita reported that the MPC's February move lifted rates to their highest in almost nine years [[n1399]], and The Banker reported Governor Glapiński taking aim at inflation [[n1361]]. The labour market gives less cover than before: Obserwator Gospodarczy reported unemployment rising for the first time in almost a year [[n1516]], even though pb.pl had reported the average wage rising 9.6% in 2021 [[n1402]], a wage base that makes second-round inflation effects more likely. Parkiet's assessment of the attack's consequences for markets [[n1522]] bears on a choice between tightening into the shock to defend the zloty and pausing to protect growth and the banks.
Playbook ✓

Action: stay underweight Polish equities, with banks the funding leg against energy-security and defence exposure elsewhere in Europe; XTB.com's list of four defence-sector stocks [[n1519]] points to defence as a theme for local investors. Trigger: further zloty weakness and fuel-price acceleration, which Agro Profil reported will speed up after the invasion [[n1568]]. What changes the call: an NBP response that stabilises the currency, a rule-of-law settlement that releases EU funds, and evidence that cash withdrawals are not turning into deposit flight; PKO Bank Polski at 35.95 PLN and the WIG20TR tracker at 31.50 PLN are the capitulation markers. ⚠ Divergence: higher rates should help Polish bank margins, yet PKO, Pekao and mBank fell between 14.52% and 16.82%; the market is pricing Ukraine exposure, deposit behaviour and Swiss-franc mortgage risk, where INFOR.PL reported falling optimism about settlements with banks [[n1558]], above the rate tailwind.
Narrative

Technology led the reversal: XLK rose 3.42% to 152.28 USD, with Microsoft +5.11%, Nvidia +6.08% and Apple +1.67% (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2022-02-24). Falling long yields likely did much of the work; Investopedia described investors fleeing stocks for gold and bonds [[n0800]], but the bond rally also lowered the discount rate on long-duration earnings. Over 20 sessions XLK is flat at -0.10%.
Reported

Nvidia's fourth-quarter fiscal 2022 release [[n0891]] remains the most recent mega-cap print, and Counterpoint Research reported global smartphone revenue hitting a record of about $450 billion in 2021 with Apple capturing its highest-ever share in the fourth quarter [[n0993]].
EPS Upside Watch

Cybersecurity is plausibly the cleanest earnings link to the war: CrowdStrike rose 13.01%, Palo Alto Networks 13.05% and Zscaler 10.02%. CrowdStrike's research on access brokers, their targets and their worth [[n1624]] describes the threat economy those budgets fight.
⚡ Breaking Convention

High-multiple software normally suffers in a crisis. Here the war pulled long yields lower and put cyber defence in focus at once, so Fortune's question of how low tech stocks can fall [[n0374]] has a different answer when the discount rate is falling.
Narrative

Communication services joined the rally, with XLC up 2.80% to 67.44 USD, but Meta Platforms (FB) remains the swing factor: +4.61% to 207.60 USD yet -29.54% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2022-02-24). Al Jazeera reported that Meta's plunge is unmatched among big tech stocks in recent years [[n0294]].
Reported

Reuters reported Facebook launching Reels globally, betting on its 'fastest growing' format [[n0444]], and Moneycontrol reported a pilot sharing ad revenues with Reels creators [[n0967]]. Reuters also reported Zuckerberg unveiling AI projects aimed at building the metaverse [[n0996]].
EPS Upside Watch

Alphabet rose 4.00%, Netflix 6.14%, Snap 5.00% and Pinterest 8.34%. Sensor Tower reported global consumer spending in the top 100 subscription apps climbing 41% to $18.3 billion in 2021 [[n1785]], support for subscription models over pure advertising if fuel prices squeeze marketing budgets.
⚡ Breaking Convention

Telecoms, the textbook defensive, lagged: AT&T fell 1.19% and Verizon 1.54%. In this war rally the market paid for growth platforms over bond-like carriers, the reverse of the standard crisis playbook.
Narrative

Financials failed to join the rebound: XLF fell 1.20% to 37.88 USD while the S&P 500 gained 1.50%. JPMorgan dropped 2.78%, Citigroup 4.03% and Bank of America 2.64% (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2022-02-24). A curve at +42 bps that has bear-flattened over 20 observations caps the margin upside banks were promised from lift-off.
Reported

Reuters reported RBC profit rising on wealth and loan growth while flagging a mortgage slowdown [[n0137]], and the Financial Times reported Morgan Stanley disclosing twin probes into big stock transactions [[n0733]]; Morgan Stanley fell 1.86%.
EPS Upside Watch

Net interest income remains the upside lever if the Fed moves in March. A Federal Reserve note on the drivers of bank supply of business loans [[n1151]] is a reminder that business lending is one channel through which a March hike would reach bank earnings.
⚡ Breaking Convention

Rate hikes are supposed to help banks. Here sanctions compliance and counterparty risk dominate; the Association of Certified Financial Crime Specialists warned that sanctions, AML and cyber risks soar [[n0662]]. Russian exposure is an operating cost before it becomes a credit loss.
Narrative

Energy equities lagged the commodity: XLE fell 0.78% to 67.11 USD while Brent rose 2.31% to 99.08 USD/bbl and WTI 0.77% to 92.81 USD/bbl (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2022-02-24). Reuters reported oil topping $105 as Russia invaded [[n1774]], before crude gave back much of that spike into the settlement.
Reported

BBC reported oil hitting a seven-year high even as shares rebounded [[n0742]]. Reuters reported Chevron monitoring the Russia situation and saying it can adjust crude supply [[n0676]], while Saipem tempered its green ambitions after a loss prompted a rethink [[n1000]].
EPS Upside Watch

With Brent +10.14% over 20 sessions against XLE's +2.93%, equities price only a fraction of the strip. Exxon Mobil fell 1.26%, Chevron 0.52% and Schlumberger 3.57%, which could leave room for estimates to catch up with crude if prices hold.
⚡ Breaking Convention

Integrated majors fell on the day GMA Network reported oil rising above $105 after the attack [[n1773]]; money moved toward technology on the day while energy equities slipped. That gap between commodity and equity is an opportunity, not a warning.
Narrative

Industrials rose 1.28% to 96.82 USD, led by defence: Lockheed Martin +1.75%, Northrop Grumman +2.44%, Raytheon Technologies (RTX) +2.18% and the ITA ETF +2.75% (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2022-02-24). Reuters reported BAE Systems saying the Russian invasion will sharpen the focus on defence [[n0665]], and Fortune reported Reddit's WallStreetBets celebrating war-friendly stocks [[n0748]].
Reported

Safran reported its full-year 2021 results [[n0140]] and, per Reuters, boosted titanium stocks to shore up its supply chain [[n0770]]. Bloomberg reported jet-engine makers looking for titanium supplies outside Russia [[n0713]].
EPS Upside Watch

Quanta Services rose 10.60%, while Caterpillar fell 1.06% and is -13.81% over 20 sessions, so the rally was selective. Deere, which Reuters said aims for bigger profit as price hikes powered an earnings beat [[n0269]], rose 1.55%.
⚡ Breaking Convention

Aerospace is not a clean war winner. Airbus fell 4.41% and Boeing has lost 9.36% over five sessions; CNN had reported airlines cancelling Ukraine flights as the threat of war grew [[n1675]]. Titanium dependence and route disruption cut against defence budgets inside the same sector.
Narrative

Consumer discretionary bounced 2.29% to 172.77 USD on Amazon +4.51% and Tesla +4.81%, but is -7.16% over five sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2022-02-24). Fuel is the war's main channel to households, and The Conversation warned of higher food and gas prices and an increased risk of recession [[n1123]].
Reported

The Business of Fashion reported TJX results missing estimates due to Omicron store closures [[n0627]]; Bloomberg reported eBay warning it is still losing customers [[n0568]]; Retail Dive reported Wayfair's revenue falling 11.4% in the fourth quarter as losses widened [[n1783]].
EPS Upside Watch

Home improvement is holding up: Reuters reported Lowe's optimistic on demand despite rising interest rates [[n0973]]. Auto Remarketing reported KAR selling its ADESA US physical auction business to Carvana for $2.2B [[n0789]]; Carvana rose 10.91%. The Verge reported Etsy hitting sellers with a 30 percent transaction-fee increase [[n0689]], a platform testing its pricing power.
⚡ Breaking Convention
The rebound was led by mega-cap platforms, not by the household. With confidence falling and fuel prices rising, discretionary spending faces a tax that the index rally ignored.
Narrative

Staples were a funding leg: XLP fell 1.72% to 73.54 USD while the S&P 500 rose, with Procter & Gamble -2.69%, Coca-Cola -1.75% and PepsiCo -1.74% (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2022-02-24). Investors sold defensives to buy beta, a rotation that works only if the energy shock stays contained; Walmart slipped 0.39%.
Reported

Reuters reported Coca-Cola HBC readying Russia contingencies as profits rose [[n0467]] and then shutting its Ukraine plant [[n0670]]. Reuters also reported Nestle temporarily closing factories and warehouses in Ukraine [[n0735]]; Nestle fell 3.15% to 115.16 CHF.
EPS Upside Watch

Pricing power is the swing factor. CBC reported more shoppers feeling inflation pressure and turning to dollar stores for deals [[n0732]], while Costco rose 2.08%, a sign that value formats can take share as budgets tighten. CSP Daily News reported private labels lifting US sales to $199 billion in 2021 [[n1887]], a structural base for trading down.
⚡ Breaking Convention

Staples usually outperform in war. They fell as money rotated toward beta, and rising input costs threaten margins faster than prices can follow: wheat rose 5.71% to 926.00 US cents/bu and corn 1.65% to 695.00 US cents/bu (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2022-02-24).
Narrative

Health care rose only 0.40% to 127.06 USD, a laggard in the rebound, with Pfizer -1.94%, Johnson & Johnson -1.91% and Merck -3.07% (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2022-02-24). The defensive bid never arrived because investors chose growth beta.
Reported

Moderna was the standout: WSJ reported it beating profit estimates on Covid-19 vaccine sales [[n0727]], and the stock rose 15.10% to 156.23 USD. BioPharma Dive reported Moderna betting on booster demand and advancing a new bivalent shot [[n0728]].
EPS Upside Watch

Managed care carries deal risk: Reuters reported the US suing to block UnitedHealth's $8 bln deal for Change Healthcare [[n0787]], and UnitedHealth fell 0.81%. Biotech rallied, with XBI up 4.58%, and Eli Lilly rose 2.00%. Fierce Biotech reported Baxter reaching an $18M settlement with the SEC over allegedly inflating income [[n1754]].
⚡ Breaking Convention

Health care's haven status failed on a war day. The sector's value now lies in idiosyncratic catalysts such as vaccine contracts and pipeline news, not in defensive flows; Fierce Pharma's report that analysts expect Eylea to 'remain king' [[n0749]] shows franchise durability still earns a premium.
Narrative

Materials split between farm inputs and metals: XLB slipped 0.29% to 81.37 USD, but CF Industries rose 5.48%, Nutrien 3.16% and Mosaic 0.33% (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2022-02-24). Bloomberg reported fertilizer shortages from Russia-Ukraine tension may hit the US growing season [[n0578]].
Reported

Reuters reported MP Materials posting higher profit as rare earth prices surge [[n0720]], while the shares rose 7.37% in the session. The Financial Post reported Agnico Eagle announcing the surprise exit of its CEO amid an earnings miss [[n0658]].
EPS Upside Watch

Aluminium rose 3.34% to 3,457.50 USD/t and palladium 2.48% to 2,498.60 USD/oz. Reuters reported oil, gas, grains and metals spiking as Russia invaded [[n1774]]; markets can attach a supply-risk premium to metals with Russian sourcing.
⚡ Breaking Convention

Yahoo Finance UK reported gold hitting a one-year high as investors flocked to a safe haven [[n0706]], with futures closing at 1,926.30 USD/oz, yet GDX fell 1.93%. Newmont fell 2.24%. Miners failed to track bullion on the day, a gap that cost discipline can close, while Freeport-McMoRan rose 2.97% even as copper slipped 0.61% to 4.45 USD/lb.
Narrative

Real estate rose 1.73% to 44.74 USD as long yields eased, but is -2.91% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2022-02-24). A lower 10Y helps REIT valuations; rising mortgage rates work against housing turnover.
Reported

MONEY reported mortgage rates rising again on February 24 [[n1919]], and Reuters reported US existing home sales accelerating as investors elbow out first-time buyers [[n1873]]. Bloomberg reported Wall Street buying starter homes to quietly become America's landlord [[n0173]], a structural bid for single-family rental.
EPS Upside Watch

Consolidation continues in niche formats: Business Wire reported SmartStop Self Storage REIT agreeing to acquire a Strategic Storage Growth Trust II portfolio in a $280 million transaction [[n0773]], and Affordable Housing Finance reported Blackstone Real Estate launching an affordable-housing company [[n0669]].
⚡ Breaking Convention

Property rallied on a war day because the shock cut long yields while high-yield credit held up; HYG gained 0.71% (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2022-02-24). Financing conditions did not tighten, which is why rate-sensitive real estate behaved like a bond proxy rather than a cyclical.
Narrative

Utilities rose 0.80% to 65.55 USD, led by NextEra Energy +4.31% while Duke Energy fell 0.65% (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2022-02-24). Vistra rose 4.18% and Southern Company 0.06%. Clean-energy equipment led harder still, with Enphase Energy +16.43% and SolarEdge Technologies +14.86%.
Reported

Uniper reported achieving its 2021 financial targets and significantly reducing economic net debt [[n0980]]. Reuters reported EDF getting $2 bln of state help over nuclear-plant outages [[n0277]], a reminder of how exposed European generators are to supply shocks.
EPS Upside Watch

Energy security now reinforces decarbonisation spending. Offshore Wind reported TenneT starting a tender for 2 GW of German offshore grid connections [[n1116]], the kind of grid build that supports regulated asset growth. Enverus examined how ORDC changes are affecting ERCOT volatility [[n0131]], a reminder that merchant power earnings are tied to scarcity pricing.
⚡ Breaking Convention

Utilities are meant to be the calm corner. With TTF at 134.32 EUR/MWh, gas-dependent European generators face margin strain, while renewables gain an energy-security argument on top of the climate one.
Narrative

European autos were among the worst-hit groups: the SXAP tracker fell 6.09% to 57.08 EUR, BMW 7.24%, Mercedes-Benz Group 6.50%, Volkswagen preference shares 5.87% and Renault 9.07% (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2022-02-24). NBC News reported the Ukraine crisis could create more woes for the auto industry [[n0979]].
Reported
Barron's reported Stellantis stock soaring as it posted a strong debut yearly profit [[n0622]], and Reuters reported scarcity and software set to power Mercedes-Benz through 2022 [[n0771]].
EPS Upside Watch

Scarcity pricing has supported margins, but supply is breaking again: BBC reported the Mini Oxford plant halted by the chip shortage [[n1739]]. Reuters reported Volkswagen and its top shareholder striking a framework deal for a Porsche IPO [[n0797]], a potential value catalyst, and Mercedes-Benz targeting the US for hands-free driving certification this year [[n0725]].
⚡ Breaking Convention

Scarcity protects margins only while plants can build. A war that adds component and energy disruption converts the 2021 pricing tailwind into lost volume, which is why strong 2021 profits failed to protect the shares.
Narrative

US semiconductors rallied while Asia's fell: SOXX rose 3.66% to 469.24 USD and ASML's US line 3.97%, but the TSMC ADR fell 3.47%, SK Hynix 6.84% and Samsung Electronics 3.77% (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2022-02-24). The Economist Intelligence Unit reported chip makers increasing investment for 2022 amid the shortage [[n1755]], and TechCrunch reported Bosch investing $296M to produce semiconductors to combat the shortage [[n1715]].
EPS Upside Watch

Barron's listed 15 chip stocks it called real bargains that keep getting cheaper [[n0652]]. TechSpot reported that Nvidia had reportedly spent $10 billion for a chunk of TSMC's 5nm capacity [[n1681]], evidence of prepaid demand.
